analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 796, National Labor Relations Board Petitioner v. Industrial Union of Marine and Shipbuilding Workers of America, AFL-CIO and its Local 22. Mr. Combe. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case is here on certiorari to the Third Circuit, which denied enforcement of the Board's order directed to the Respondent Shipbuilding Workers Union and its Local 22. The basic question is whether a union violates Section 8B1A of the National Labor Relations Act by disciplining a member for filing an unfair labor practice charge against the union with the National Labor Relations Board before he has exhausted internal union procedures for the resolution of his dispute. Now, the basic facts are these. Early in 1964, Edwin Holder, a member of Local 22 and employed by the United States Lines Company as a ship painter, filed charges with the local accusing its president of conduct violative of the International Union's Constitution. When the local's trial board determined that the president was not guilty of the charges, Holder, without pursuing his intra-union procedures, the International's Constitution provided for appeals to the general membership of the local, and then to the general executive board of the International, and finally to the National Convention, filed unfair labor practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board covering the same subject matter. He filed two charges. He filed one against the union, alleging that the union had caused United States lines to discriminate against him in employment because of his concerted activities in violation of Sections 8B2 and 8B1A of the National Labor Relations Act. He filed a companion charge against the company, United States lines, alleging that the company had discriminated against him because of his union activity in violation of Sections 8A1 and 8A3 of the National Labor Relations Act. After the filing of these charges, which I might say upon investigation by the board's regional director would dismiss for lack of evidence, the union accused Holder of violating the provision of the union constitution, which provided that every member shall exhaust all remedies and appeals within the union before he shall resort to any court or other tribunal outside of the union. He was found guilty of having violated this provision by filing charges with the National Labor Relations Board and was expelled from union membership. Holder thereupon filed another charge with the National Labor Relations Board, which forms the basis for this proceeding, alleging that the union, by expelling him for having filed his first charge with the board, violated Section 8B1A of the act, which I will get to in a moment. Is it clear, Mr. Cohn, that nothing in this case affected his employment relationship with U.S. lines? That is correct. There is no dispute that his employment was not affected. The board, applying its SCURA decision, in which it held that a union had violated Section 8B1A by fining a member who had filed charges against the board, found that the union here had violated Section 8B1A and entered an appropriate remedial order. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit set aside the board's order. Its decision is in conflict with what the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia did in the Roberts case, upholding a comparable board order. Now, Section 8B1A, which this Court is well familiar with, provides that it shall be an unfair labor practice for a labor organization to restrain or coerce employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in Section 7 of the Act. I might say that the statutory provisions are set forth at beginning pages 39 of the government's brief. Now, there's a proviso to Section 8B1A that says that this paragraph shall not impair the right of a labor organization to prescribe its own rules with respect to the acquisition or retention of membership therein. Now, I wish to acknowledge at the outset that I've got a problem with this proviso, and I have a further problem with this Court's decision in Alice Chalmers' only last term, which I hope I can overcome. But before I get to that, I would just like to deal momentarily with the subsidiary contention that there's no impairment of a Section 7 right here to begin with. Now, I think that the courts have pretty clearly established, and even the court below acknowledges, that the right to file a charge with the National Labor Relations Board, even though it is not specifically enumerated in Section 7 of the Act, is included in there by necessary implication for the simple reason that, as this Court has recognized only most recently, early this term in the Nash case, the board can only act when a charge is filed. And therefore, as a necessary precondition to vindicating all the other rights that are specifically enumerated in Section 7, there must be the right to file a charge. Secondly, I think that it is also well settled that a charge, since it merely sets in motion the board machinery, doesn't have to have the specificity of a formal plea. And that the charge here, although the Court below seemed to think to the contrary, was certainly specific enough to show that a holder was complaining of a violation of his Section 7 rights. So that, I think that... Section 7 protects only concerted activities, doesn't it? Well, that contention is raised by the union, and I think that that is... Well, it is. That's correct. I mean, that's what its language says. Well, it says employees shall have a right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to engage in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining, or other mutual aid or protection, and shall also have the right to refrain from any or all of such activities. Now, there is no question that an individual has a right to complain of union activity that interferes with his right to refrain from engaging in union activity. I mean, it doesn't have to be concerted in the sense that it's a grievance that he's alleging, not only for himself, but for other people. What Holder was complaining about here was that the union was discriminating, or causing the employer to discriminate against him in the Department of Employment Opportunities because of a position that he had either taken or failed to take with regard to the union. There was no question about that, so far as the act is concerned, an individual employee has a right to be a charging party to file a charge under section of an unfair labor practice. But the question is whether or not that particular right is one of the rights protected by Section 7 of the Act. And it has to be in order for you to prevail, doesn't it? Yes, but all I'm saying is that the kind of complaint that Holder made is the garden-variety kind of complaint, if there were merit to it, that would be found to violate 8B-2 if you could prove that the union was discriminating against him for the reason that he alleged, or that the company was violating 8A-3 if they acquiesced in the union's causing the discrimination. Secondly, there's also a matter as to whether or not the union had failed to process a grievance alleging this problem in good faith, which would raise a problem as to whether there was a duty of the union's, a violation of the union's duty of fair representation, which would give you an 8B-1A violation. All I'm saying is that although there may be situations at the periphery as to whether the filing of a charge is a Section 7 activity or not, the sort of thing that Holder was complaining of here, if the evidence sustained his contention, would have been clear violations of the statute, and I think that that is all that we have to show to get in the ballpark here. Now, I'd like to turn to the one other thing on the Section 7 end of it, and that is that if the individual is protected in his right to file a charge, he has the right to file the charge under the Act as promptly as possible. As this Court pointed out in a decision earlier this term, there is no requirement in the National Labor Relations Act for the exhaustion of administrative remedies. As a matter of fact, Section 10A of the Act says that the Board's power shall not be affected by any other private means of adjustment, and Section 10B of the Act, which sets a six-month statute of limitations period, indeed encourages the prompt filing of charges. So that we start then, at least in our view of it, with a situation where the union by expelling Holder for filing charges with the Board promptly, without exhausting his internal union remedy, in a very real sense, has restrained or coerced him in exercising freely the right that Section 7 would give him to file such a charge promptly, irrespective of whether on investigation it proved to have merit as long, at least as there was no showing that he acted in bad faith, and there is none here. So then we come to the problem as to whether or not this restraint or coercion is legal restraint or coercion, and that brings us to the proviso to 8B1A and to this Court's decision in the Ellis Chalmers case. Now, for the union, this is a very easy case. They read the terms of the proviso, and they say that this exhaustion requirement was a membership requirement which Holder agreed to when he joined the union. By violating this membership requirement, the union could discipline him. And that ends the ballgame for them because they apply the plain meaning rule, and they say how plainer can you get something that fits within the terms of the statute. Now, I admit that that is a persuasive argument. However, this Court has oftentimes cautioned that the plain meaning rule, particularly with respect to Section 8B1A, is not a very reliable guide as to the reach of the provision, that you have to look at the statute in the light of its legislative history and, even more importantly, in the light of the other provisions of the statute, because Congress, in enacting 8B1A, was trying to fit it into a unified statutory pattern. Now, when we look at the unified statutory pattern, what do we find? Well, we find, first of all, as I've indicated, that under Section 10B of the Act, the Board cannot act unless a charge is filed. You look at the employer side of the picture, and you find that employer coercion in respect to the filing of charges is prohibited. It's not only prohibited specifically under Section 8A4, but it has been held, even by the Court below, that such employer coercion has been held to violate the general terms of Section 8A1 of the statute, which bars employer, in general terms, restraint of coercion in the exercise of Section 7 rights. Now, looking at those provisions, this Court, in the Nash case, earlier this term, said this indicates that Congress intended that an individual would be free of all coercion in respect to the filing of unfair labor practice charges. As a matter of fact, the Court said employer and union coercion, and refer it to the Roberts case. Nash, to be sure, did not involve union coercion and involved the question as to whether or not the state of Florida's policy of denying an individual unemployment compensation because he had filed charges was in conflict with the scheme of the Act. So then, we say in the light of this statutory pattern, it is reasonable for the Board to read the general restraint and coercion terms of 8B1A as affording the same protection against union coercion in respect to the filing of charges which is that 8A1 of the Act provides against employer coercion. Now, in the Alice Chalmers case, which was decided last term, this Court held that 8B1A did not bar a union from fining those of its members who refused to heed the union strike call and seeking to collect those fines by state court suits. Now, in reaching that conclusion, the Court relied upon two principal things as I read the decision. One, that the right to strike was an important weapon in the union's economic arsenal, and unless it had power to find strikebreakers, the right to strike would be substantially impaired. And secondly, that as the Court read the legislative history of Section 8B1A and its proviso, it indicated that Congress did not propose any limitation with respect to the internal affairs of a labor union. Now, I should point out that, as the Court is well aware, that Alice Chalmers was a 5-4 decision, and Mr. Justice White, in his concurring opinion, indicated that he did not read the majority opinion as privileging any union rule, no matter how unreasonable or unenforceable on its face. It appeared to be. Now, apart from that, however, we've submitted that, as Judge Fahey pointed out for the Court of Appeals in the Roberts case, that a union rule that would penalize employees for filing charges with the board goes beyond the area of internal union affairs that Congress was concerned about in enacting the, in providing an exemption under 8B1A. As Judge Fahey put it, such a rule goes beyond the internal affairs of the union and into the public domain. Wouldn't that be equally true of a decertification petition filed by a member, and yet the board is, how has the board differentiated that situation? You're quite right in pointing out that the board has differentiated a decertification petition. Well, that does not involve internal union affairs any more than this case, does it? Well, I think that the decertification petition case is a troublesome one. I think that it partakes of much of the same aspects that I'm talking about with respect to a charge. However, there is, there is this difference, and that is that with respect to a charge, the individual is complaining that the union has violated his statutory right. With respect to a decertification petition, he is attacking the very existence of the union itself, and a decertification petition is going to... Attack the existence of the union itself, as you well know. Well, he is in the sense that... Unlike the automobile workers, they're not going to be put out of existence if they don't represent a particular local and a particular small town. Well, you have the further problem that it's well acknowledged that a union is entitled to protect itself against this loyalty in its ranks. And what a decertification petition means that you're going to have an election campaign, you're going to... And the question is whether the union has to keep to its bosom a defector while this election campaign is going on. Now, this is what the board thought tipped the balance the other way. I think... There's nothing... You can't point to anything in the language of the statute that would differentiate that case from this one, can you? No, I cannot. Just a matter of value judgment by the board in terms of public policy. Is that it? I believe so. However, I do not think that we have to decide the correctness of that... of the board's position in that case at this time. Well, it rather tests the correctness of the board's decision in this case. I suggest. Well, I won't... I won't dispute that. But, as you can appreciate, Your Honor, whenever you have competing policies as you do have here, on the one hand, the policy in favor of giving protection to internal union affairs, and on the other hand, the policy of keeping the channels of the board open, there's going to come a point where those policies are going to get very close together, and you could very easily go on either side of that line. Now, I think that the decertification case is in that area. I think it gets very, very close. I think that the charge case, however, and the Alice Chalmers case are... it's easier to separate them out. Now, I just want... We both agree it's no easier in terms of the way the statute is written. No, I think not, except with this exception, that with respect to the filing of a charge, Section 10B makes it perfectly clear that that a board cannot act unless a charge is filed. You also have 8A1 of the act, which bars employer coercion for interfering with the Section 7 rights. Well, you have 8A4, which expressly makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to do this, and the act is entirely silent with respect to unions doing it. Well, that is correct, however... You have that additional argument in this case that you don't have in the decertification case against your positions. That is correct, and I'm not minimizing the difficulties that I have with the decertification case, but I submit that we're entitled to prevail here, even if we are wrong in the decertification case, and I would like to... Well, does the employer have the same degree of interest in the two situations? Does the individual union member have the same degree of interest, same directness of interest in the two situations? Well, in the charge case, he certainly has a very immediate interest in that what he is complaining about is that the union has violated his statutory right. Now, with respect to the decertification petition, he has a real interest, I would have to acknowledge in the sense that he is saying that this year... The person has an interest, but it's no different from the interest of all other members. Well, that is correct, Your Honor. That is correct. In that sense, there is a difference. However, I should like to point out that not only does the filing of a charge get into the public domain, but it has been recognized by scholars in the field that these restrictions in union constitutions against resort to the courts and other outside tribunals are acknowledged to be against public policy. As Archibald Cox pointed out, the restriction is against public policy. No private organization should be permitted to restrict any person's access to the courts of justice, no less than restrict his right to petition the legislature to communicate with a member of Congress. You mentioned the proviso. Yes, Your Honor. of your argument. Well, what I meant to say was that reading the proviso in the light of section 10b of the act, the necessity for the board to have a charge before it can act, the provision in 8A1 that would prescribe employer coercion in respect to the filing of charges. The fact that a restriction on resort to the board is commonly acknowledged to be contrary to public policy, the board is reasonable in saying that the literal terms of the proviso were not intended to encompass a union restriction on the filing of charges because it is contrary, such a reading of the proviso would be contrary to the scheme of the remainder of the act and to recognize public policy. What force do you give the proviso? I would say that the proviso would apply to other normal area of internal union affairs such as the kind of union rule that you had in Alice Chalmers but not to a union rule such as the one that we have here that goes beyond the area of internal union affairs and attempts to choke off the procedures of the board. Now, I would like to say in the moments that are remaining to me that there is a big distinction between a union restriction on resort to public tribunals and the rule of judicial administration. There is a well-recognized principle of judicial administration in these union suits that says that when a union comes to a court, the court, if it is persuaded that it has an adequate union remedy, will stay its hand and remit the individual to his union tribunal. We say that that is a far cry from a union sanction because there the individual has a chance to go to an impartial tribunal, for the impartial tribunal to make a judgment as to whether the union procedure is in fact adequate, and then can remit them. If, on the other hand, the tribunal is satisfied that the procedure is inadequate, it can give the individual member immediate relief without requiring the member to guess as to whether or not he's got a situation that can wait or can't wait, and if he guesses wrong, union discipline sticks. For those reasons, we submit that the court erred in denying enforcement of the board's order in this case. Mr. Goldstein? Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. Before saying anything else, I should like to point out that nowhere in the record of this case, is there anything to show that the union failed to process a grievance for Mr. Holder, or any of the other facts respecting the detail of his alleged complaint against the union? I should also like to say that in so far as the board argues public policy here, I think we have two considerations. First, even if you call expulsion from a union, restraint or coercion, in the sense in which those words are used in section 8b1a, you do not, in this case, have that restraint or coercion used to block completely or to punish for entry into the board's processes. You have it only as a rule which under the statute can delay, and by the statute I'm referring to the Landry of Griffin Act, section 101a4, can delay access to the board for four months at the most. in the second place, the Congress has already adopted a public policy on this matter, notwithstanding all of the scholarly attempts to split hairs about whom the proviso on section 101a4 of the Landry and Griffin Act applies to. It is perfectly clear as is set forth in the opinion of the court below, and as is set forth in our briefs, that the best reasoning is that the public policy would permit a union itself or a court or a board to impose only a four-month delay. With these preliminary attempts to answer only one or two of the statements made by my brother, I should like to say that to me, the most striking aspect of this case is that the board under the guise of interpreting section 8b1a has, in effect, legislated a new unfair labor practice. I say this because the pertinent statutes and their legislative history, as well as this court's opinion, last term in the Alice Chalmers case, make it so eminently clear that the union conduct which the board in this case condemns is not violative of section 8b1a. And I believe that my statement is warranted in addition by the fact that this evidence is such clear and preponderant proof that such conduct is not an unfair labor practice, that for 17 years the board, its general counsel, and the courts uniformly so held. Indeed, only a few months before the board decided, the progenitor of our case, namely the Scora case. The board stated, after reviewing the relevant legislative history, that it had not been empowered by Congress to police a union decision that a member is or is not in good standing, or to pass judgment on the penalties a union may impose on a member, so long as the penalty does not impair the member status as an employee. And it is to be remembered that in this case, as Mr. Combe admits for the board, Mr. Holder's status as an employee was not changed one whit. The board said this in the case of the Wisconsin Motor Company, which was affirmed a few weeks ago, by the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit under the name of Schofield v. the NLRB. I should like now, if I may, to list some of the items of evidence that demonstrate that Mr. Holder's expulsion from his union is not an unfair labor practice. Before doing so, Before you do that, Mr. Moshe, what is the chronology here? Mr. Holder did file a complaint with his local union, did he not? Against the president, alleging that the president had violated the national union's constitution. Yes, sir. And do you have the date when he did that? That was... Well, let me ask you this. what I want to know is, did the local decide that issue within or outside of the four-month period? Oh, within. Within. And without waiting further, Mr. Holder then immediately filed his charge based on the same facts with the labor board. Before going into the listing these items of evidence, I should like to emphasize that the board itself found that Holder was expelled not simply because he filed a charge with the board, but because by doing so he violated his duty under his union's constitution to proceed with the internal remedies provided by that constitution for adjusting his grievances against the local union. I don't know if I may interject at this point. Mr. Carter, may I ask you, do I gather that you do agree with Mr. Combe that the four-month limitation in 101 applies here? I would, Mr. Justice Prevents, sir. May I ask you then, of course, the local, I gather, disposed of this within the four-month period? I think you just said. That's right, sir. But would it have been possible for him to have exhausted his other remedies through the international within the four-month period? The appeal to the General Executive Board, yes, that would have been very readily done because there are time limitations upon the length of time that the General Executive Board may consume in passing on a case. And it did happen, by the way, that when he appealed from his expulsion by the local union, the General Executive Board very promptly heard the case and very promptly decided that. Would he have had a right under the union procedures to go to the convention over the... Yes, he would. Now, he could not have done that within four months. Certainly not. Now, there, however, I would say to you, sir, that unless the court, as a matter of its own jurisprudential discretion, said you've got to exhaust your remedies before you come here, he would have been free under Section 101A4 of the Landrum Griffin Act to come right to the board and we could have done nothing about it. Well, let's see. What you mean, then, is had he at least done everything he could have done within the four months? After he'd exhausted such steps as he could exhaust within four months, even though there were other steps that he couldn't as going to the convention, then he would have been free to go to the board. Precisely, sir. And I would say this. The union certainly would not have been in any position to discipline him in any wise, whether by suspension, fine, or expulsion, if, having utilized its internal processes for four months, and not having gotten a final resolution satisfied treaty... Can you tell me briefly, Mr. Goldstein, what are the time limits your union puts on this exhaustion? What are the steps? First, you have to go to the local, I gather. That's right, sir. And is there a time limit fixed? For the local to act? Yes. No, sir, there is not. But, and there is no time either for the local membership to pass on an appeal from its executive board's decision. But it seems to me, sir, that none of that is material here, because I freely admit that once four months have passed, the man is free. And in this case, the four months, Mr. Justice Ford, and Mr. Justice Brennan, had not elapsed. Otherwise, we would have done nothing. How much time did elapse? I'm in part. How much time did elapse here after he... The best that I can determine, Mr. Chief Justice, from the record as it stands, is that there were about two or three months before, between the date of his charge against the union, the president, and the final disposition of his appeal to the membership, two or three months at the moment, so that he still had time to go to the general executive board, and just, Judge Hastie below points out that although that could be a protracted proceeding, it need not necessarily be so as exemplified by the fact that in his appeal to the general executive board from his own expulsion, he got a very expeditious determination. Judge Hastie points that out. Now let me, if I may, list some, not all, of the items of evidence as I see it, which make it clear and should have made it clear to the board that there was not in this case a Section 8B1A violation. Section 8A4 of the Act makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to visit a reprisal upon an employee because that employee has filed charges under the Act. It would seem perfectly simple, possibly too simple logic to say that had Congress intended in 1949 when it added Section 8B, the list of union unfair labor practices, to the Wagner Act to proscribe similar action by union in a clear statement to that effect in Section 8B. Indeed, the House, in passing the Taft-Hartley Act, included in it a Section 8C5, which did make it an unfair labor practice for a union to fine or penalize any member because he made charges or instituted proceedings against the union. The Conference Committee, however, deleted this section from the House's bill, and the bill was passed without it. So that, as Mr. Justice Stewart pointed out, there is no provision in Section 8B with respect to unions that is cognate to Section 8A4 with respect to employers. The second piece of evidence, because of the absence of such a specific provision in Section 8B, the Board seeks to use Section 8B1A as a substitute net in which to catch its fish. The body of that section makes it an unfair labor practice for a union to restrain or coerce employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in Section 7. Here again, I feel I might rather sit down because I think your honors have all of the facets of this case very firmly in your grasp because, as Mr. Justice Stewart pointed out, Section 7, however, guarantees only the right to engage or to refrain from engaging in concerted activities. It does not, and perhaps not even by implication, let alone explicitly guarantee any employee the right to file an unfair labor practice charge. Well, if a union member is fired out of the union, is it your position that he's not deprived of his right to conduct concerted activities in Section 7? Is that your point? My point? Here, a man belongs to a union, and as a union member, he conducts, he's engaged as one of many in collective bargaining and concerted activities. And the union fires him, says you're no longer a member. And I tell you, your point is that despite that, the section, language of Section 7 is not implicated. On the other hand, it could be argued that if you kick a man out of the union, that you deprive him of, you at least curtail or invade his right to engage in concerted activities. Mr. Justice Forrest, I must concede to you that you are impinging on a member's right to engage in concerted activities when you throw him out of the union, which is the instrumentality for carrying on the concerted activities. But I think if one goes farther than that, one is guilty of circular reasoning because... Well, I sure don't want to be guilty of that. Well, you might catch up with yourself, sir. Because what happens there is, if we adopt your theory, is that the board is punishing a union or may punish a union every time that union, for no matter what reason, expels or suspends a member. Because every time it does so, it is, under your reasoning in which I concur, affecting the member's concerted activities or opportunities to engage in. But that is... Perhaps you've just demonstrated a proposition which I have heard, that one man's circle is another man's triangle. What the board is doing here, however, is saying, not that the union interfered with holders' concerted activities or right to engage in them by expelling him, but that interfered with his right to engage in the concerted activity of filing a charge by expelling him. And that's an entirely different thing. There is... I must concede, as we do in our brief, that the filing of a charge may be something in connection with a concerted activity. For example, seven men are trying to organize a plant. The employer discriminates against them. They file a charge. Certainly, they are engaging in concerted activity when they file that charge. One man is treated in a fashion of by his employer that he doesn't like. He files a charge. That certainly is not concerted activity. Suppose a union fires a man from membership... We never filed our... ...from membership in the union. Terminates his membership in the union. And suppose he does not have a remedy under the unfair labor practice provision of the act. Can he go... Does he have a remedy in the court? Would you ask me for that? Can he get... Go to court? Does he have... Can the court grant an injunction on proper showing to compel the union to reinstate him? Since 1959, he has had a federal right to do that. Before that, he had a state right under the Landrum-Griffin Act. You have your Bill of Rights of Members. One of those bills of rights... One of the rights, rather, in that bill is the right set forth in Section 101A4 of a member to sue either the officers of his union or his union. And, as a matter of fact, one of the things we have to consider in this case, I submit to your honors, is whether in that enactment, 101A4, and also Section 102, that's right, of that act, Congress has not made it perfectly clear that the Board simply has no jurisdiction over a case in which a member of the union, on expulsion from that union, seeks reinstatement.
